title: What Reformed mean by imputed Christ’s righteousness
source_text: XIX. Huc autem, non alio respiciunt Scholae Reformatae Doctores, quum dicunt Christi justitiam nobis imputari, nosque justificari & justos esse coram Deo per imputatam Christi justitiam, non vero per justitiam ullam quae nobis inhaereat. His enim & similibus formulis nihil aliud significare volunt quam Christi obedientiam usque ad mortem crucis, Deo Patri nostro nomine praestitam, ita nobis a Deo donari ut vere nostra censeatur, eamque esse unicam & solam illam justitiam propter quam & cujus merito & virtute absolvimur a reatu peccatorum nostrorum, & in Dei filios ac vitae aeternae haeredes adoptamur: Nec ullam in nobis esse justitiam, aut ulla bona opera quibus beneficia tanta promereamur; quaeve ferre possint districtum judicii divini examen, si Deus juxta legis suae rigorem nobiscum agere velit. Ac proinde, quum severum Dei tribunal cogitamus, & maledictionem transgressoribus a lege intentatam, juxta terribilem illam clausulam, Maledictus omnis qui non permanserit in omnibus quae scripta sunt in libro legis hujus, ut faciat ea; nihil nos ei posse opponere, nisi Christi meritum & satisfactionem; in qua sola, peccatorum conscientia exterriti, tutum adversus iram divinam perfugium, & animarum nostrarum pacem & solatium invenire possumus.
pass_a_gloss: To this, and not elsewhere, the doctors of the Reformed schools look when they say that Christ’s righteousness is imputed to us, and that we are justified and are just before God by the imputed righteousness of Christ, not by any righteousness that inheres in us. By these and like formulas they mean nothing other than that Christ’s obedience unto the death of the cross, rendered to God the Father in our name, is so given to us by God that it is truly reckoned ours, and that it is the unique and only righteousness on account of which and by whose merit and virtue we are absolved from the guilt of our sins and adopted as God’s children and heirs of eternal life; and that there is in us no righteousness or any good works by which we merit such great benefits, or that can bear the strict examination of divine judgment if God wills to deal with us according to the rigor of his law. And therefore, when we think of God’s severe tribunal and the curse threatened by the law to transgressors according to that terrible clause, Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things written in the book of this law to do them, we can oppose nothing to it except Christ’s merit and satisfaction; in which alone, terrified in conscience of sins, we can find a safe refuge against divine wrath and the peace and consolation of our souls.
pass_b_english: Reformed “imputed righteousness” means Christ’s cross-obedience given as truly ours—the sole ground of absolution and adoption.
No inherent works can stand law’s rigor; conscience flees only to Christ’s merit.
